system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2142-04-27 14:00:00 to 2142-04-30 17:13:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes and bilateral below-knee amputations was admitted after her visiting nurse noted a small erosion with exposed bone on her right amputation site. She denied pain, fever, or systemic symptoms and had been recently discharged two days prior for a brief episode of vomiting. Examination revealed a 0.5 cm area of serous drainage over the tibial tuberosity without erythema or purulence. Laboratory results showed mild leukocytosis and elevated glucose. She was treated with IV antibiotics and wound care. Surgery was recommended to cover the exposed bone, but the patient declined immediate intervention and planned to return the following week. She was discharged home with nursing support, oral Bactrim for 14 days, and instructions to monitor for signs of infection. Follow-up was arranged for surgical evaluation.
problems: Diabetes with neurological manifestations, type I [juvenile type], not stated as uncontrolled
Amputation of limb(s) causing abnormal patient reaction, or later complication, without mention of misadventure at time of operation

Discharge Instructions:
DISCHARGE INSTRUCTIONS FOLLOWING Revision Below the Knee 
AMPUTATION 

.

This information is designed as a guideline to assist you in a 
speedy recovery from your surgery. Please follow these 
guidelines unless your physician has specifically instructed you 
otherwise. Please call our office nurse if you have any 
questions. Dial 911 if you have any medical emergency.

.
Antibiotics:
You will be leaving the hospital with 10 days of antibiotics: 
you should take 10 days of oral ciprofloxacin and 10 days of 
oral flagyl. In addition, you should receive 10 days of IV 
vancomycin through your PICC line. Your PICC line can be removed 
after you finish your 10 day home course of antibiotics.

ACTIVITY: 

.

There are restrictions on activity. On the side of your 
transmetatarsal amputation you are non weight bearing for ___ 
weeks. You should keep this amputation site elevated when ever 
possible. 

No driving until cleared by your Surgeon.

.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

.

Redness in or drainage from your leg wound(s).

.

New pain, numbness or discoloration of your foot or toes.

.

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever 
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus 
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these 
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR. 

.

Exercise:

.

Limit strenuous activity for 6 weeks. 

.

Do not drive a car unless cleared by your Surgeon. 

.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next ___ days. 

.

Try to keep leg elevated when able.

.

BATHING/SHOWERING: 

.

You may shower immediately upon coming home. No bathing. A 
dressing may cover youre amputation site and this should be 
left in place for three (3) days. Remove it after this time and 
wash your incision(s) gently with soap and water. You will have 
sutures, which are usually removed in 4 weeks. This will be done 
by the Surgeon on your ___ appointment.

.

WOUND CARE:

.

Sutures / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are 
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for staple 
removal. 

.

When the sutures are removed the doctor may or may not place 
pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision. These will 
stay on about a week and you may shower with them on. If these 
do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off with warm 
water and soap in the shower.

. 

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for 
four weeks after surgery. 

.

MEDICATIONS: 

.

Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the 
medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a 
new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every 
three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary. 

.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you 
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check 
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel 
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may 
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite 
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small 
balanced meals throughout the day.

CAUTIONS:

.

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is 
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of 
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you 
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse 
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

.

Avoid pressure to your amputation site.

.

No strenuous activity for 6 weeks after surgery. 

.

DIET:

.

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively. 
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent 
meals may be preferred. 

.

For people with vascular problems we would recommend a 
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and 
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile 
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in 
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a 
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that 
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to 
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the 
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density 
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's 
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred 
or get a referral from your doctor. 

.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight 
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on 
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be 
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new 
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get 
a referral from your doctor. 

.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may 
request a referral from your doctor.

___ APPOINTMENT: 

.

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your 
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the 
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood 
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to 
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated! 

.

Please call the office on the first working day after your 
discharge from the hospital to schedule a ___ visit. This 
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days 
after discharge. Normal office hours are ___ 
through ___.

.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR 
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE.

You will be leaving the hospital with 10 days of antibiotics: 
you should take 10 days of oral ciprofloxacin and 10 days of 
oral flagyl. In addition, you should receive 10 days of IV 
vancomycin through your PICC line. Your PICC line can be removed 
after you finish your 10 day home course of antibiotics.

ACTIVITY: 

.

There are restrictions on activity. On the side of your 
transmetatarsal amputation you are non weight bearing for ___ 
weeks. You should keep this amputation site elevated when ever 
possible. 

No driving until cleared by your Surgeon.

.

PLEASE CALL US IMMEDIATELY FOR ANY OF THE FOLLOWING PROBLEMS:

.

Redness in or drainage from your leg wound(s).

.

New pain, numbness or discoloration of your foot or toes.

.

Watch for signs and symptoms of infection. These are: a fever 
greater than 101 degrees, chills, increased redness, or pus 
draining from the incision site. If you experience any of these 
or bleeding at the incision site, CALL THE DOCTOR. 

.

Exercise:

.

Limit strenuous activity for 6 weeks. 

.

Do not drive a car unless cleared by your Surgeon. 

.

No heavy lifting greater than 20 pounds for the next ___ days. 

.

Try to keep leg elevated when able.

.

BATHING/SHOWERING: 

.

You may shower immediately upon coming home. No bathing. A 
dressing may cover youre amputation site and this should be 
left in place for three (3) days. Remove it after this time and 
wash your incision(s) gently with soap and water. You will have 
sutures, which are usually removed in 4 weeks. This will be done 
by the Surgeon on your ___ appointment.

.

WOUND CARE:

.

Sutures / Staples may be removed before discharge. If they are 
not, an appointment will be made for you to return for staple 
removal. 

.

When the sutures are removed the doctor may or may not place 
pieces of tape called steri-strips over the incision. These will 
stay on about a week and you may shower with them on. If these 
do not fall off after 10 days, you may peel them off with warm 
water and soap in the shower.

. 

Avoid taking a tub bath, swimming, or soaking in a hot tub for 
four weeks after surgery. 

.

MEDICATIONS: 

.

Unless told otherwise you should resume taking all of the 
medications you were taking before surgery. You will be given a 
new prescription for pain medication, which can be taken every 
three (3) to four (4) hours only if necessary. 

.

Remember that narcotic pain meds can be constipating and you 
should increase the fluid and bulk foods in your diet. (Check 
with your physician if you have fluid restrictions.) If you feel 
that you are constipated, do not strain at the toilet. You may 
use over the counter Metamucil or Milk of Magnesia. Appetite 
suppression may occur; this will improve with time. Eat small 
balanced meals throughout the day.

CAUTIONS:

.

NO SMOKING! We know you've heard this before, but it really is 
an important step to your recovery. Smoking causes narrowing of 
your blood vessels which in turn decreases circulation. If you 
smoke you will need to stop as soon as possible. Ask your nurse 
or doctor for information on smoking cessation.

.

Avoid pressure to your amputation site.

.

No strenuous activity for 6 weeks after surgery. 

.

DIET:

.

There are no special restrictions on your diet postoperatively. 
Poor appetite is expected for several weeks and small, frequent 
meals may be preferred. 

.

For people with vascular problems we would recommend a 
cholesterol lowering diet: Follow a diet low in total fat and 
low in saturated fat and in cholesterol to improve lipid profile 
in your blood. Additionally, some people see a reduction in 
serum cholesterol by reducing dietary cholesterol. Since a 
reduction in dietary cholesterol is not harmful, we suggest that 
most people reduce dietary fat, saturated fat and cholesterol to 
decrease total cholesterol and LDL (Low Density Lipoprotein-the 
bad cholesterol). Exercise will increase your HDL (High Density 
Lipoprotein-the good cholesterol) and with your doctor's 
permission, is typically recommended. You may be self-referred 
or get a referral from your doctor. 

.

If you are overweight, you need to think about starting a weight 
management program. Your health and its improvement depend on 
it. We know that making changes in your lifestyle will not be 
easy, and it will require a whole new set of habits and a new 
attitude. If interested you can may be self-referred or can get 
a referral from your doctor. 

.

If you have diabetes and would like additional guidance, you may 
request a referral from your doctor.

___ APPOINTMENT: 

.

Be sure to keep your medical appointments. The key to your 
improving health will be to keep a tight reign on any of the 
chronic medical conditions that you have. Things like high blood 
pressure, diabetes, and high cholesterol are major villains to 
the blood vessels. Don't let them go untreated! 

.

Please call the office on the first working day after your 
discharge from the hospital to schedule a ___ visit. This 
should be scheduled on the calendar for seven to fourteen days 
after discharge. Normal office hours are ___ 
through ___.

.

PLEASE FEEL FREE TO CALL THE OFFICE WITH ANY OTHER CONCERNS OR 
QUESTIONS THAT MIGHT ARISE. 

 
Followup Instructions:
___

radiology_notes.text:
HISTORY:  Cough, preop for BKA.

PA AND LATERAL CHEST RADIOGRAPH.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  There is prominence of the pulmonary vasculature with apical
redistribution.  The heart is top normal in size.  No pneumothorax or pleural
effusions present.

IMPRESSION:  Pulmonary congestion or edema.  Top normal-size heart.

INDICATION:  ___ female with new basilic PICC placement.

COMPARISON:  PA and lateral chest radiograph from ___ as well as
correlation with CT of the chest without contrast from ___.

FINDINGS:  Right basilic PICC is seen with its tip projecting approximately 9
cm beyond the likely location of the cavoatrial junction into the right
atrium.  There is no evidence of pneumothorax.  There is a region of right
upper lobe peribronchovascular opacification with air bronchograms and that is
likely chronic post-infectious changes and correlates with the findings on CT
and previous findings on radiographs.  There is no new focal consolidation to
suggest acute pneumonia.  There is a band of linear atelectasis in the left
mid lung.  The heart is top normal in size, however, unchanged from prior. 
Pleural surfaces are unremarkable.  There is no pneumothorax or pleural
effusion.  There is an IVC filter projecting over the likely location of the
inferior vena cava.

IMPRESSION:
1.  PICC tip likely 9 cm beyond the cavoatrial junction.  Recommendation made
the ___ nurse to withdraw by 9 cm.
2.  No radiologic evidence of acute cardiopulmonary process.

SINGLE AP PORTABLE VIEW OF THE CHEST

REASON FOR EXAM:  Assess line that has been pulled back 9 cm.

Comparison is made with prior study performed five hours earlier.

Left PICC tip is in the mid SVC.  Mild cardiomegaly.  Peribronchial opacities
in the right upper lobe and lower lobes bilaterally are unchanged.  There is
an IVC filter.  There is no pneumothorax or pleural effusion.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee, one of your surgical doctors. You’re here because your right amputation stump is infected. We’re going to treat this with IV antibiotics and prepare you for surgery tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I don’t feel any pain. I only get phantom pain, like my leg is still there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense because of your neuropathy. But we can see signs of infection—there’s exposed bone and drainage. That’s why we need to do a revision of the amputation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time I said no. But now I guess it has to be done.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s important to fix the exposed bone to prevent worse infection. We’ll do the surgery tomorrow. Tonight, you’ll get IV antibiotics—vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on insulin? My sugars have been high lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started you on a sliding scale insulin. Your blood sugar was low when you came in—49—but we gave you dextrose. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had trouble with high sugars before. My A1c was 12% last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something we’ll keep working on. The diabetes team will help adjust your insulin while you’re here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today because of your chronic cough. It shows some fluid in the lungs, but your heart size is normal. Nothing urgent, but we’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had this cough for a while. Is it from my heart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. With heart failure, fluid can build up in the lungs. Your ejection fraction is 40%, so we’ll manage your fluids carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood sugar was very high overnight—up to 600. So we started an insulin drip to bring it down safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no, that’s bad. I didn’t feel anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we monitor it. You’re on the drip now to keep it between 100 and 150. We’ll switch back to injections after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. Am I still having surgery today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as soon as you’re stable. You’re NPO—nothing by mouth after midnight—for the procedure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, you’re back from surgery. The revision BKA went well—no complications. They resected part of the tibia and closed the stump cleanly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel groggy, but okay. Is the infection gone now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The infected tissue was removed, but you’ll still need antibiotics for 10 days to make sure it doesn’t come back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I be on IV the whole time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for vancomycin. We’ll set up a PICC line tomorrow so you can get it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my pain? I have some aching.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started oral oxycodone and sustained-release morphine. Let us know if it’s not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m also a bit nauseous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the pain meds. We’ll give you something for nausea and adjust your pain plan if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We placed the PICC line this morning in your arm. But the first X-ray showed it was too deep—tip in the right atrium.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, so we pulled it back 9 cm. A new X-ray confirmed it’s now in the right spot—mid superior vena cava. You’re all set.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re working on it. Your labs show your sodium and potassium are low, but close to your baseline. We gave you fluids and kayexylate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia for years. Is that why my hemoglobin is low?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your hemoglobin was 9.4 on admission, now it’s improved to 11.2. That’s good progress after surgery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The diabetes team adjusted your insulin. You’ll stay on the sliding scale, plus Lantus twice daily and Humalog at lunch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Can I eat now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’re on a regular diabetic diet. Try small meals if your appetite is low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked a random vancomycin level today—it came back high at 36.8.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It increases risk of kidney issues. So we held your evening dose and you’ll skip tomorrow’s morning dose. We’ll check a proper trough before the next one.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, so I’m not getting the antibiotic for a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a short pause. The other antibiotics—cipro and flagyl—will continue.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your family mentioned rehab, but you told Dr. Patel you’d prefer to go home with nursing support?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’m more comfortable at home. My nurse knows me well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. We’ll arrange home health for wound care, IV antibiotics, and monitoring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re medically ready to go home. We’ll discharge you today with services.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What do I need to watch for?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call us if you have fever over 101, increased redness, pus, or new pain. Keep the leg elevated and avoid pressure on the stump.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the PICC line?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Home health will flush it daily. After 10 days of IV vancomycin, it can be removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need help with the meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll take oral cipro and flagyl for 10 days, plus pain meds as needed. We’ve simplified your metoprolol to 25 mg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gabapentin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Now 400 mg three times a day. Lower dose to protect your kidneys, especially with the vancomycin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. When’s my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call the office in the next few days to schedule your visit—7 to 14 days after discharge. We’ll check your wound and remove sutures.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And no driving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not until cleared by your surgeon. Also, no heavy lifting over 20 pounds for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I won’t smoke. I know it’s bad for my circulation.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. It really helps healing. You’re doing well. We’ll get the discharge papers ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The home health nurse will arrive this afternoon. You can go home once they confirm they’re on the way.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel ready.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Take care, and call us with any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Thanks for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’ll see you in clinic soon. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will assist you to the wheelchair. Discharge is official.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 58-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and bilateral below-knee amputations was admitted for a revision below-the-knee amputation due to a chronic infection of the right stump with exposed bone. She was started on IV vancomycin, ciprofloxacin, and metronidazole upon admission. An insulin drip was initiated to manage hyperglycemia, later transitioned to a sliding scale. She underwent an uncomplicated revision BKA and had a PICC line placed for outpatient antibiotic therapy, which required repositioning confirmed by chest X-ray. A high vancomycin level prompted a temporary hold in dosing. She was discharged home with home health services on oral and IV antibiotics, pain management, and detailed wound care instructions, with follow-up scheduled in 7–14 days.
